theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Function Generators, Synthesis and Specifications

A laboratory function generator is built around a loop of two blocks: an integrator and a comparator with hysteresis (Schmitt trigger). The comparator output is a square wave; integrating it gives a triangle whose peaks switch the comparator back, so both waveforms come out together. A diode break-point shaping network then rounds the triangle into a sine wave with a few tenths of a percent to about 1 % distortion. The charging current of the integrator is set by a control voltage, so the same instrument can be swept in frequency (a voltage-controlled generator), and the output stage adds amplitude control, a DC offset, a step attenuator and a 50 Ω output resistance.
Common kinds of signal generator and what distinguishes them:
items: Audio-frequency (AF) sine generator: low-distortion sine, typically a Wien-bridge oscillator, about 10 Hz to 100 kHz.
RF signal generator: an LC or synthesized oscillator with AM/FM modulation and a calibrated output attenuator reaching microvolt levels, for testing receivers.
Function generator: square, triangle and sine (plus ramp and pulse) from one integrator-comparator loop, with a sweep input.
Pulse generator: independent control of repetition rate, pulse width, delay, amplitude and rise/fall times, for digital and switching tests.
Sweep generator: frequency moves automatically between two limits, so a filter or amplifier response can be displayed directly on an oscilloscope.
Arbitrary waveform generator (AWG) and DDS synthesizer: samples stored in memory are played out through a DAC, giving any shape with crystal-referenced frequency.

rows: Transient response, slew rate, tilt and ringing
Linearity checks, sweep and PWM reference
Harmonics with nD = integer are missing

theoryAdd.text: Modern generators obtain their frequency by synthesis rather than from a free-running oscillator. In a phase-locked loop (PLL) synthesizer a voltage-controlled oscillator is divided by a programmable number N and its phase is compared with a crystal reference of frequency f_ref; the loop filter adjusts the VCO until the divided output equals f_ref, so f_out = N f_ref and the step size (channel spacing) is f_ref. In direct digital synthesis (DDS) an n-bit phase accumulator adds a tuning word M on every clock pulse; the accumulator value addresses a sine look-up table whose samples go to a DAC and a low-pass reconstruction filter. Both inherit the fractional (ppm) accuracy of their crystal reference.

theoryAdd.plainText: DDS with an n-bit accumulator: f_out = M·f_clk / 2^n; resolution Δf = f_clk / 2^n (PLL: f_out = N·f_xtal / R)

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 1 - PLL synthesizer
Crystal 12.8 MHz, reference divider R = 512
  f_ref = 12.8 MHz / 512 = 25 kHz  (= channel spacing)
Wanted output 90 MHz: N = 90 MHz / 25 kHz = 3600
Crystal tolerance ±2.5 ppm is carried to the output:
  error = 90 MHz × 2.5 × 10^-6 = ±225 Hz
Next channel (N = 3601) = 90.025 MHz

Worked example 2 - DDS tuning word
Clock f_clk = 125 MHz, accumulator n = 28 bits
  Resolution = 125 MHz / 2^28 = 125e6 / 268 435 456 = 0.466 Hz
Wanted f_out = 10 kHz:
  M = f_out × 2^n / f_clk = 10e3 × 268 435 456 / 125e6 = 21 474.8 -> 21 475
  Actual f_out = 21 475 × 125e6 / 2^28 = 10 000.08 Hz
Highest usable output < f_clk / 2 = 62.5 MHz (Nyquist); about 40 % of f_clk in practice

1 µHz to 20 MHz; ±20 ppm with a crystal reference
10 % to 90 % transition of a square or pulse
A few ns to tens of ns; t_r ≈ 0.35 / bandwidth
Output level range and DC shift
Up to 10 V p-p into 50 Ω, ±5 V offset
Fraction of the period spent high

theoryAdd.text: A generator with a 50 Ω output behaves as an EMF in series with 50 Ω. Into a matched 50 Ω load the voltage is half the open-circuit value; into a high-impedance load such as an oscilloscope input it is almost the full EMF. Many instruments display the amplitude assuming a 50 Ω load, so a setting of 1 V p-p reads about 2 V p-p on a high-impedance scope. Also remember that dBm is a power level referred to 1 mW, so converting it to volts needs the load resistance.

For synthesizer questions write the relation first: PLL step = f_ref and f_out = N f_ref; DDS step = f_clk / 2^n (n = accumulator bits) and f_out = M × step. For waveform questions remember odd harmonics at 1/n for a square wave, 1/n² for a triangle, and all harmonics for a sawtooth.

questions.questionText: In a conventional analogue function generator, the sine-wave output is usually obtained by:
options: Shaping the triangle wave with a diode break-point network
Passing the square wave through a crystal
questions.explanation: The integrator-comparator loop produces square and triangle waves; a non-linear diode network rounds the triangle peaks into an approximate sine wave.

questions.questionText: In a function generator, the block that converts the square wave from the comparator into a triangle wave is:
questions.explanation: Integrating a constant positive or negative voltage produces a linear ramp, so a square wave becomes a triangle wave.

questions.questionText: The VCG (voltage-controlled generator) or sweep input of a function generator allows the operator to:
options: Change the output impedance from 50 Ω to 600 Ω
Add a DC offset to the output
Vary the output frequency with an external control voltage
Change the waveform from sine to square
questions.explanation: The control voltage sets the integrator charging current and hence the frequency, so an external ramp can sweep the frequency.

questions.questionText: A ±10 V square wave at 1 kHz drives an ideal integrator with RC = 1 ms. The peak-to-peak amplitude of the resulting triangle wave is:
questions.explanation: During each half period (0.5 ms) the output ramps at V/RC = 10 V/1 ms = 10 V/ms, so it changes by 10 × 0.5 = 5 V peak-to-peak.

questions.questionText: A pulse generator gives pulses 20 µs wide with a period of 100 µs. The duty cycle is:
questions.explanation: Duty cycle = t_on/T = 20/100 = 20 %.

questions.questionText: A pulse generator is set to 50 kHz with a 25 % duty cycle. The pulse width is:
questions.explanation: T = 1/50 kHz = 20 µs; pulse width = 0.25 × 20 µs = 5 µs.

questions.questionText: A rectangular pulse train switches between 0 V and 5 V with a duty cycle of 40 %. Its average (DC) value is:
questions.explanation: V_avg = D × V_high = 0.4 × 5 = 2 V (3.16 V would be the RMS value, 5√0.4).

questions.questionText: The rise time of a pulse from a pulse generator is conventionally measured between:
options: 50 % of the rising edge and 50 % of the falling edge
The start of the pulse and its peak overshoot
questions.explanation: Rise time is the time for the edge to go from 10 % to 90 % of its final amplitude; the 50 %-to-50 % interval is the pulse width.

questions.questionText: A square wave passes through an amplifier whose bandwidth is 100 MHz. Using t_r ≈ 0.35/BW, the rise time of the output is about:
Which statement about the frequency spectrum of an ideal symmetrical (50 % duty) square wave is correct?
options: It contains all harmonics with equal amplitude
It contains only odd harmonics, the nth harmonic having 1/n of the fundamental amplitude
questions.explanation: The Fourier series is (4A/π)(sin ωt + (1/3) sin 3ωt + (1/5) sin 5ωt + ...): odd harmonics only, falling as 1/n.

questions.questionText: For an ideal symmetrical triangle wave, the amplitude of the third harmonic relative to the fundamental is about:
questions.explanation: Triangle-wave harmonics fall as 1/n²: 1/3² = 1/9 = 11.1 %. (33.3 % is the 1/n law of a square wave.)

questions.questionText: Compared with a square wave and a triangle wave, a sawtooth (ramp) waveform is distinguished by containing:
questions.explanation: A sawtooth lacks half-wave symmetry, so its Fourier series contains every integer harmonic with amplitude proportional to 1/n.

questions.questionText: A symmetrical square wave alternates between +5 V and −5 V. The RMS value of its fundamental (sinusoidal) component is about:
questions.explanation: Fundamental peak = 4A/π = 4 × 5/π = 6.37 V; RMS = 6.37/√2 = 4.50 V.

questions.questionText: A generator's sine output contains a 10 V (RMS) fundamental, a 0.6 V second harmonic and a 0.8 V third harmonic. Its total harmonic distortion is:
questions.explanation: THD = √(0.6² + 0.8²)/10 = 1.0/10 = 10 %. Adding the harmonics directly would wrongly give 14 %.

questions.questionText: The strongest harmonic of a signal generator's sine output is specified as −40 dBc (relative to the carrier/fundamental). As a fraction of the fundamental voltage this harmonic is:
questions.explanation: Voltage ratio = 10^(−40/20) = 0.01 = 1 % of the fundamental.

questions.questionText: A function generator with a 50 Ω output resistance produces 4 V p-p on open circuit. When it is connected to a 50 Ω load, the voltage across the load is:
questions.explanation: Voltage divider: V_L = 4 × 50/(50 + 50) = 2 V p-p.

questions.questionText: A generator has an open-circuit output of 10 V and an internal resistance of 50 Ω. The voltage it delivers to a 1 kΩ load is about:
A signal generator with a 50 Ω output resistance has an open-circuit (EMF) output of 2 V RMS and is connected to a matched 50 Ω load. The power delivered to the load, in dBm, is about:
questions.explanation: Load voltage = 1 V RMS; P = 1²/50 = 20 mW; 10 log(20 mW/1 mW) = 13.0 dBm.

questions.questionText: A sweep generator is set to sweep logarithmically from 20 Hz to 20 kHz. The number of octaves covered is about:
questions.explanation: Octaves = log2(20 000/20) = log2(1000) = 9.97, about 10 (the same span is 3 decades).

questions.questionText: A PLL frequency synthesizer has a reference (comparison) frequency of 100 kHz and a programmable divider N = 455. Its output frequency is:
questions.explanation: f_out = N × f_ref = 455 × 100 kHz = 45.5 MHz.

questions.questionText: A PLL synthesizer divides a 10 MHz crystal by R = 100 to obtain its reference and uses a feedback divider N = 1234. The output frequency is:
questions.explanation: f_ref = 10 MHz/100 = 100 kHz; f_out = N f_ref = 1234 × 100 kHz = 123.4 MHz.

questions.questionText: An integer-N PLL synthesizer must produce output frequencies in steps of 25 kHz. Its comparison (reference) frequency must be:
questions.explanation: With f_out = N f_ref, changing N by one moves the output by f_ref, so f_ref equals the step size, 25 kHz.

questions.questionText: A DDS generator has a 100 MHz clock and a 32-bit phase accumulator. Its frequency resolution is about:
A DDS generator uses a 100 MHz clock and a 32-bit phase accumulator. The tuning word M needed for an output of 1 MHz is about:
According to the sampling theorem, the highest output frequency a DDS generator clocked at 100 MHz can theoretically produce is:
questions.explanation: Each output cycle needs at least two samples, so f_out(max) = f_clk/2 = 50 MHz; practical designs stay near 40 % of f_clk.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a building block of a direct digital synthesis (DDS) generator?
options: An LC tank circuit that sets the output frequency
A DAC followed by a low-pass filter
questions.explanation: DDS is digital: the accumulator, look-up table, DAC and reconstruction filter set the frequency from the clock; no tuned LC tank determines it.

questions.questionText: A main advantage of a DDS signal generator over a PLL synthesizer is:
options: Very fine frequency resolution with fast, phase-continuous frequency changes
No need for a clock or reference oscillator
Output frequencies above the clock frequency
questions.explanation: Changing the tuning word changes frequency on the next clock with no loop settling and in sub-hertz steps; DDS still needs a clock, has spurs, and is limited below f_clk/2.

questions.questionText: The feedback loop of a PLL frequency synthesizer contains a phase detector, a loop filter, a programmable frequency divider and a:
options: Quartz crystal in the feedback path
questions.explanation: The phase detector error, filtered by the loop filter, tunes a VCO whose divided output is compared with the reference.

questions.questionText: A 100 MHz output is synthesized by a PLL from a 10 MHz crystal reference whose accuracy is ±5 ppm. The maximum frequency error of the output is:
questions.explanation: A PLL multiplies the reference, so the fractional error is unchanged: 100 MHz × 5 × 10^-6 = ±500 Hz (±50 Hz is the error of the 10 MHz reference itself).

questions.questionText: Compared with a basic function generator, an RF signal generator used for receiver testing is characterised by:
options: Built-in AM/FM modulation and a calibrated attenuator giving very low output levels
An output frequency limited to the audio range
A high output impedance of about 1 MΩ
questions.explanation: Receiver tests need a modulated RF carrier whose level can be set accurately down to microvolts, hence modulation facilities and a calibrated attenuator with a 50 Ω output.

questions.questionText: A signal generator output of 1 V is passed through its step attenuator set to 60 dB. The output voltage is:
questions.explanation: Voltage ratio = 10^(60/20) = 1000, so the output is 1 V/1000 = 1 mV.

questions.questionText: A sweep generator is most commonly used to:
options: Measure the DC resistance of a resistor
Generate a precise DC reference voltage
Measure the power factor of a load
Display the frequency response of an amplifier or filter
questions.explanation: Its frequency moves continuously between two limits, so plotting the device output against the sweep gives the frequency response directly.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a specification of a pulse generator?
questions.explanation: Pulse generators are specified by repetition rate, width, delay, amplitude and rise/fall time; Q factor describes resonant circuits.

questions.questionText: An arbitrary waveform generator (AWG) produces its output by:
options: Adjusting the Q of an LC tank circuit
Clipping a sine wave with Zener diodes
Reading stored sample values from memory and converting them with a DAC
questions.explanation: An AWG holds the waveform as a table of samples in memory and plays them out through a DAC at the sample clock rate, so any shape can be defined.

questions.questionText: An arbitrary waveform generator runs at 1 GS/s (10^9 samples per second) and a waveform uses 1000 samples per cycle. The output frequency is:
questions.explanation: f = sample rate/points per cycle = 10^9/1000 = 1 MHz.

questions.questionText: An AWG has a 14-bit DAC spanning 2 V peak-to-peak full scale. When it generates a 0.5 V peak-to-peak sine wave, the number of DAC levels actually used is about:
questions.explanation: LSB = 2 V/2^14 = 122 µV; levels used = 0.5 V/122 µV = 4096, i.e. only about 12 bits of resolution.

questions.questionText: The sawtooth waveform of a signal generator is the natural choice for:
options: The carrier of an AM broadcast transmitter
Measuring the harmonic distortion of an amplifier
The horizontal time-base sweep of a cathode-ray oscilloscope
questions.explanation: A linear ramp moves the CRO beam at constant speed across the screen, and the fast retrace returns it for the next sweep.

questions.questionText: A low-frequency square wave is applied to an amplifier and the flat tops of the output show a noticeable tilt (sag). This indicates:
options: A limited low-frequency response (high lower cut-off frequency)
questions.explanation: Sag on the flat parts comes from coupling capacitors discharging, i.e. poor low-frequency response; slow or rounded edges would instead show poor high-frequency response.

questions.questionText: The period of a signal from a generator is measured as 2.5 µs. Its frequency is:
A signal generator is set to give a sine wave of 1 V RMS. Its peak-to-peak value is about:
A function generator produces a ±2 V square wave and a +1 V DC offset is then added. The output now swings between:
questions.explanation: The offset shifts the whole waveform up by 1 V: −2 + 1 = −1 V and +2 + 1 = +3 V; the average becomes 1 V.

questions.questionText: A rectangular pulse train has a duty cycle of 25 %. Which harmonics are completely absent from its spectrum?
questions.explanation: The nth harmonic amplitude is proportional to sin(nπD)/n; with D = 0.25 it is zero when n/4 is an integer, so the 4th, 8th, ... vanish, while the 2nd and 6th remain.

questions.questionText: Which statement about an electronic signal generator (oscillator) is correct?
options: It needs an AC input signal of the same frequency to produce an output
It produces a periodic output without any input signal, converting DC supply power into AC signal power
It uses negative feedback to sustain its output
It creates energy, so it needs no power supply
questions.explanation: An oscillator sustains its output through positive feedback and draws the energy for the AC output from its DC supply; no input signal is needed.

questions.questionText: To measure the slew rate of an op-amp, the signal generator should apply:
options: A small-amplitude sine wave at very low frequency
A large-amplitude square wave, observing the slope of the output edges
A triangle wave of a few millivolts
questions.explanation: Slew rate is the maximum rate of change of the output, seen when a large step forces the output to ramp; its value is ΔV/Δt of the output edge.

questions.questionText: A sawtooth generator's ramp rises for 4 ms and the flyback (retrace) takes 1 ms. The frequency of the sawtooth is:
questions.explanation: T = sweep + flyback = 4 + 1 = 5 ms; f = 1/5 ms = 200 Hz (ignoring the flyback would give 250 Hz).

questions.questionText: A generator is set to deliver +10 dBm into a 50 Ω load with a sine wave. The peak-to-peak voltage across the load is about:
